transitivity: both — transitive (chew your food), intransitive (chew slowly)
gloss: To break food up with your teeth before swallowing it.
examples: *Chew* your food slowly — it helps digestion.
The puppy *chewed* the corner off my shoe.
She sat *chewing* gum and staring out the window.

transitivity: both — transitive (swallow a pill), intransitive (it hurts to swallow)
gloss: To make food or drink go down your throat.
examples: *Swallow* the pill with plenty of water.
He *swallowed* the last bite and stood up.
She winced, *swallowing* the bitter medicine.

transitivity: both — transitive (munch popcorn), intransitive (munch on chips)
gloss: To eat something noisily and steadily, usually a crunchy snack.
examples: The kids *munch* popcorn through the whole movie.
He *munched* on carrot sticks while he waited.
I could hear someone *munching* chips behind me.
contrast: Verbs ending in -ch add -es in the third person: he *munches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (nibble a cracker), intransitive (nibble at the cheese)
gloss: To eat something in small, gentle bites.
examples: Mice *nibble* the corners of the cereal boxes.
She *nibbled* a cracker and pushed the rest away.
He spent the party *nibbling* on cheese.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *nibbled*, *nibbling*.

gloss: To eat something quickly and hungrily.
examples: Teenagers *devour* whatever is in the fridge.
He *devoured* two plates of pasta in ten minutes.
The cake had been *devoured* before I got a slice.

gloss: To eat small amounts of food between meals.
examples: I *snack* too much when I study.
We *snacked* on almonds during the drive.
She has been *snacking* all afternoon.
contrast: Takes **on** before the food: *snack on* nuts, never 'snack nuts'.

gloss: To eat a large, festive meal with great enjoyment.
examples: Every November they *feast* on turkey and pie.
We *feasted* until nobody could move.
The guests were *feasting* while the cook rested.
contrast: Takes **on**: *feast on* lobster.

gloss: To eat dinner, especially in a restaurant or in a formal setting.
examples: They *dine* out every Friday.
We *dined* on the terrace as the sun went down.
We were *dining* when the power went out.
contrast: The silent -e disappears before -ing: *dining* with one n.

gloss: To break food down in the stomach so the body can use it.
examples: Babies cannot *digest* solid food yet.
He never fully *digested* that fried chicken.
Sit still for a while — your body is *digesting* lunch.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (dy-JEST); the noun *a digest* on the first.

gloss: To eat or drink something, especially in a measured amount.
examples: Americans *consume* a lot of sugar.
He *consumed* three liters of water that day.
The label shows how many calories you are *consuming*.

gloss: To enjoy the taste of something slowly and fully.
examples: *Savor* the first sip — that coffee was expensive.
She *savored* every bite of the dessert.
He sat by the window, *savoring* his soup.
contrast: American *savor*, *savored*, *savoring*; the British spelling is *savour*.

transitivity: both — transitive (taste the sauce), intransitive (it tastes salty)
gloss: To try a small amount of food or drink, or to have a particular flavor.
examples: *Taste* it before you add any salt.
I *tasted* the sauce and reached for the pepper.
This soup *tastes* like it needs garlic.
contrast: Flavors follow **like** or a bare adjective: it *tastes like* lemon, it *tastes* bitter.

gloss: To try a small portion of a food or drink to see what it is like.
examples: Shoppers *sample* the cheese at the counter.
We *sampled* four kinds of honey.
He is *sampling* every beer on the list.

gloss: To move your tongue across something, usually to taste it.
examples: Don't *lick* the spoon and put it back.
The dog *licked* the plate clean.
She was *licking* frosting off her fingers.

transitivity: both — transitive (slurp your soup), intransitive (stop slurping)
gloss: To eat or drink something with a loud sucking noise.
examples: Please don't *slurp* your soup at the table.
He *slurped* the last of the noodles.
Someone behind me was *slurping* iced coffee.

transitivity: both — transitive (sip your tea), intransitive (sip at the glass)
gloss: To drink something in small mouthfuls.
examples: *Sip* it slowly — that tea is boiling.
She *sipped* her wine and said nothing.
He sat *sipping* coffee at the counter.
contrast: One vowel plus one consonant doubles the p: *sipped*, *sipping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (gulp your milk), intransitive (he gulped nervously)
gloss: To swallow a drink or food quickly in large mouthfuls.
examples: Don't *gulp* your milk like that.
He *gulped* the water and asked for more.
She was *gulping* air after the run.

gloss: To drink a whole drink quickly without stopping, in informal speech.
examples: College kids *chug* soda at parties.
He *chugged* a bottle of water after practice.
They were *chugging* lemonade in the heat.
contrast: The g doubles: *chugged*, *chugging*.

gloss: To brown bread or nuts with dry heat, or to raise a glass in someone's honor.
examples: *Toast* the bread while I fry the eggs.
We stood and *toasted* the newlyweds.
She is *toasting* almonds for the salad.

gloss: To satisfy your thirst with a drink.
examples: Nothing *quenches* thirst like cold water.
The lemonade *quenched* our thirst in seconds.
He drank soda after soda without *quenching* anything.
contrast: Almost always with *thirst*; -ch takes -es: *quenches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (starve yourself), intransitive (the cattle starved)
gloss: To suffer or die from a lack of food.
examples: I'm *starving* — when is dinner?
Whole villages *starved* that winter.
He has *starved* himself on that diet for weeks.
contrast: In everyday speech *I'm starving* just means 'very hungry'.

gloss: To go without food for a period of time, often for religious or medical reasons.
examples: Many people *fast* during Ramadan.
She *fasted* for twelve hours before the blood test.
He has been *fasting* since sunrise.
contrast: Spelled like the adjective *fast* 'quick', but the meanings are unrelated.

gloss: To limit what you eat in order to lose weight.
examples: She *diets* every January.
He *dieted* for months before the wedding.
I'm *dieting*, so no cake for me.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t is not doubled: *dieted*, *dieting*.

gloss: To want a particular food or drink very badly.
examples: Pregnant women often *crave* strange foods.
I *craved* salt for days after the flu.
He has been *craving* his mother's soup.

transitivity: both — transitive (the smoke choked us), intransitive (he choked on a bone)
gloss: To be unable to breathe because food or drink is blocking your throat.
examples: Cut the grapes so the baby doesn't *choke*.
He *choked* on a fish bone at dinner.
She started *choking* and someone slapped her back.
contrast: Takes **on** before the food: *choke on* a bone.

transitivity: both — transitive (vomit blood), intransitive (he vomited twice)
gloss: To bring food up from the stomach and out through the mouth.
examples: The bad oysters made him *vomit*.
She *vomited* twice during the night.
He was pale and *vomiting* by morning.
contrast: First-syllable stress, so the t is not doubled: *vomited*, *vomiting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (burp the baby), intransitive (he burped loudly)
gloss: To let air come up noisily from the stomach through the mouth.
examples: It's rude to *burp* at the table.
The baby *burped* and fell asleep.
She is *burping* him after his bottle.

gloss: To let saliva run out of your mouth, often because food smells or looks good.
examples: Dogs *drool* when they smell bacon.
The baby *drooled* all over his bib.
We stood *drooling* in front of the bakery window.

gloss: To fill a food tightly with a mixture, or to fill yourself with too much food.
examples: *Stuff* the peppers with rice and ground beef.
She *stuffed* the turkey the night before.
We were *stuffed* after the third course.
contrast: The participle is an everyday adjective: *I'm stuffed* means 'I've eaten too much'.

transitivity: both — transitive (serve the soup), intransitive (they serve until ten)
gloss: To give food or drink to someone, or to attend to customers.
examples: They *serve* breakfast until eleven.
The waiter *served* us in about five minutes.
Dinner is being *served* in the next room.

transitivity: both — transitive (order a salad), intransitive (have you ordered yet?)
gloss: To ask for food or drink to be brought to you.
examples: I always *order* the same thing here.
We *ordered* two coffees and a pastry.
She is *ordering* for the whole table.

gloss: To arrange in advance for a table, room, or seat to be kept for you.
examples: Let's *reserve* a table for eight o'clock.
He *reserved* the corner booth for her birthday.
This table is *reserved* for the party of six.

gloss: To arrange a table, room, or ticket in advance.
examples: Should I *book* a table for Saturday?
She *booked* the restaurant weeks ago.
They are fully *booked* tonight.
contrast: Everyday synonym of *reserve*; *fully booked* means no places are left.

gloss: To show someone to a place to sit, especially in a restaurant.
examples: The host will *seat* you in a moment.
They *seated* us by the window.
Please wait to be *seated*.

gloss: To welcome someone when they arrive.
examples: A hostess *greets* every guest at the door.
The owner *greeted* us by name.
He was *greeting* customers all evening.

transitivity: both — transitive (tip the waiter), intransitive (Americans tip generously)
gloss: To give extra money to someone who has served you.
examples: In the States you *tip* about twenty percent.
We *tipped* the driver five dollars.
She left without *tipping*.
contrast: The p doubles: *tipped*, *tipping*.

gloss: To send or hand someone a statement of what they owe.
examples: They *bill* you at the end of the meal.
The restaurant *billed* us twice for the wine.
We are being *billed* for a bottle we never opened.
contrast: In an American restaurant you ask for the *check*; the *bill* is more often a utility or hotel invoice.

gloss: To suggest something as good or suitable.
examples: What do you *recommend* tonight?
The waiter *recommended* the salmon.
This place was *recommended* by a friend.
contrast: One c, two m's: *recommend*, *recommended*.

gloss: To put an idea or option forward for someone to consider.
examples: Can you *suggest* a good place for brunch?
She *suggested* sharing a dessert.
He is *suggesting* that we split the check.
contrast: Followed by *-ing* or by *that*: *suggest going*, *suggest that we go* — never 'suggest me to go'.

transitivity: both — transitive (deliver a pizza), intransitive (they deliver on weekends)
gloss: To bring food or goods to the place where someone wants them.
examples: They *deliver* until midnight.
The pizza was *delivered* cold.
Someone is *delivering* groceries this afternoon.
contrast: The r is never doubled: *delivered*, *delivering*.

transitivity: both — transitive (cater a wedding), intransitive (they cater to vegans)
gloss: To provide and serve food for an event.
examples: Who is going to *cater* the wedding?
A local deli *catered* the office party.
They have been *catering* events for twenty years.
contrast: With **to** it means 'serve someone's tastes': the menu *caters to* vegetarians.

gloss: To invite people to a meal or event and take care of them.
examples: We *host* Thanksgiving every other year.
They *hosted* twenty people for dinner.
She is *hosting* a wine tasting on Friday.

transitivity: both — transitive (entertain guests), intransitive (they entertain often)
gloss: To have guests in your home and give them food and company.
examples: They *entertain* a lot in the summer.
We *entertained* his parents last weekend.
The dining room is used only for *entertaining*.

gloss: To get food or a meal ready.
examples: I'll *prepare* the salad while you grill.
She *prepared* dinner for twelve.
The chef is *preparing* a tasting menu.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *preparing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (share a dessert), intransitive (we always share)
gloss: To divide food or a dish between two or more people.
examples: Let's *share* an appetizer.
We *shared* a slice of cheesecake.
They are *sharing* one plate between three of them.
contrast: The person takes **with**: *share it with* me.

transitivity: both — transitive (cook dinner), intransitive (the rice is cooking)
gloss: To prepare food using heat.
examples: He *cooks* dinner on weeknights.
She *cooked* rice and beans for everyone.
Something is *cooking* — I can smell it.

transitivity: both — transitive (bake a cake), intransitive (the pie is baking)
gloss: To cook food in an oven with dry heat.
examples: I *bake* bread on Sundays.
She *baked* a cake for his birthday.
The potatoes are *baking* now.

transitivity: both — transitive (boil the eggs), intransitive (the water is boiling)
gloss: To heat a liquid until it bubbles, or to cook food in bubbling water.
examples: *Boil* the water before you add the pasta.
I *boiled* two eggs for breakfast.
The soup has been *boiling* for ten minutes.

transitivity: both — transitive (fry the fish), intransitive (the onions are frying)
gloss: To cook food in hot oil or fat.
examples: Don't *fry* the fish too long.
He *fried* onions in butter.
She is *frying* bacon for the sandwiches.
contrast: The -y becomes -ie- in *fries* and *fried*, but stays in *frying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (grill the burgers), intransitive (we grilled all afternoon)
gloss: To cook food on a rack over direct heat, usually outdoors.
examples: We *grill* burgers every Fourth of July.
He *grilled* chicken and corn.
They were *grilling* in the backyard when it rained.

transitivity: both — transitive (roast a chicken), intransitive (the beef is roasting)
gloss: To cook meat, vegetables, or nuts in an oven or over a fire.
examples: *Roast* the vegetables at four hundred degrees.
She *roasted* a chicken with lemon.
The coffee beans are *roasted* locally.

transitivity: both — transitive (steam the broccoli), intransitive (the rice is steaming)
gloss: To cook food over boiling water, using the vapor.
examples: *Steam* the broccoli for four minutes.
I *steamed* the dumplings instead of frying them.
The rice is *steaming* on the back burner.

transitivity: both — transitive (simmer the sauce), intransitive (let it simmer)
gloss: To cook something gently in liquid kept just below boiling.
examples: Let the sauce *simmer* for an hour.
She *simmered* the stock all afternoon.
The beans have been *simmering* since noon.

gloss: To fry food quickly in a little hot fat, stirring as it cooks.
examples: *Sauté* the garlic before you add the tomatoes.
He *sautéed* mushrooms in olive oil.
She is *sautéing* onions for the soup.
contrast: A French loanword: American recipes keep the accent — *sautéed*, *sautéing*.

gloss: To cook food gently in barely simmering liquid.
examples: *Poach* the eggs for three minutes.
She *poached* salmon in white wine.
He likes his eggs *poached*, not fried.
contrast: -ch takes -es: *poaches*.

gloss: To heat or cook food in a microwave oven.
examples: *Microwave* it for ninety seconds.
He *microwaved* last night's pizza.
She is *microwaving* a bowl of soup.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *microwaving*.

gloss: To heat food again after it has cooled.
examples: *Reheat* the sauce over low heat.
I *reheated* the leftovers for lunch.
The pasta is *reheating* in the oven.

gloss: To make food or drink moderately hot.
examples: *Warm* the milk before you add the yeast.
She *warmed* the rolls in the oven.
He is *warming* soup on the stove.

transitivity: both — transitive (heat the oil), intransitive (the oven is heating)
gloss: To make something hot, especially food or liquid.
examples: *Heat* the oil until it shimmers.
I *heated* the leftovers in a pan.
The skillet is *heating* now.

transitivity: both — transitive (chill the wine), intransitive (the dough chills overnight)
gloss: To make food or drink cold, usually in a refrigerator.
examples: *Chill* the wine for an hour.
She *chilled* the dough overnight.
The dessert is *chilling* in the fridge.

gloss: To keep food cold in a refrigerator so that it stays fresh.
examples: *Refrigerate* the sauce after opening.
I *refrigerated* the soup overnight.
Fresh pasta must be *refrigerated*, not left out.

transitivity: both — transitive (defrost the chicken), intransitive (the steaks defrosted)
gloss: To let frozen food warm up until it is no longer frozen.
examples: *Defrost* the chicken in the fridge, not on the counter.
She *defrosted* the shrimp under cold water.
The steaks are *defrosting* on a plate.

transitivity: both — transitive (thaw the turkey), intransitive (the berries thawed)
gloss: To become unfrozen, or to let frozen food do so.
examples: Let the fish *thaw* before you cook it.
The berries *thawed* in about an hour.
The turkey is still *thawing*.
contrast: Rhymes with *law*: the final w is not pronounced.

transitivity: both — transitive (marinate the beef), intransitive (let it marinate)
gloss: To soak food in a seasoned liquid before cooking it.
examples: *Marinate* the beef for at least an hour.
He *marinated* the chicken in yogurt and spices.
The ribs have been *marinating* since morning.

gloss: To add salt, pepper, or spices to food.
examples: *Season* the soup at the very end.
She *seasoned* the fish with lemon and dill.
He is *seasoning* the steaks now.
contrast: Takes **with** for the spice: *season it with* cumin.

gloss: To scatter small amounts of something over food.
examples: *Sprinkle* sugar over the berries.
He *sprinkled* cheese on the pasta.
She is *sprinkling* salt on the fries.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *sprinkling*.

gloss: To decorate a dish or a drink with a small piece of food.
examples: *Garnish* the soup with parsley.
The bartender *garnished* the drink with a lime wedge.
Each plate was *garnished* with mint.
contrast: False friend: English *garnish* is a decoration, not Russian гарнир — that is a *side dish*. And -sh takes -es: *garnishes*.

gloss: To pour a thin stream of liquid slowly over food.
examples: *Drizzle* olive oil over the salad.
She *drizzled* honey on the yogurt.
He is *drizzling* melted chocolate on the cake.

gloss: To put something on the surface of a dish as a finishing layer.
examples: *Top* the pie with whipped cream.
They *topped* the burger with a fried egg.
The sundae came *topped* with nuts.
contrast: The p doubles: *topped*, *topping*.

gloss: To spread butter on bread or over a cooking dish.
examples: *Butter* the pan before you pour the batter.
He *buttered* four slices of toast.
She is *buttering* rolls for the table.
contrast: First-syllable stress, so no doubling: *buttered*, *buttering*.

gloss: To cut food into pieces with quick, heavy strokes of a knife.
examples: *Chop* the onion finely.
He *chopped* parsley for the sauce.
She is *chopping* vegetables for the stew.
contrast: The p doubles: *chopped*, *chopping*.

gloss: To cut food into thin, flat pieces.
examples: *Slice* the bread thin.
He *sliced* tomatoes for the sandwich.
She is *slicing* cheese for the board.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *slicing*.

gloss: To cut food into small cubes.
examples: *Dice* the potatoes so they cook evenly.
He *diced* an onion and a carrot.
She is *dicing* peppers for the salsa.

gloss: To chop food into very small pieces.
examples: *Mince* two cloves of garlic.
She *minced* fresh ginger for the marinade.
He is *mincing* herbs with a heavy knife.
contrast: In American English chopped meat is *ground beef*, not 'mince'.

transitivity: both — transitive (peel a potato), intransitive (the skin peels off easily)
gloss: To remove the skin from a fruit or vegetable.
examples: *Peel* the carrots before you grate them.
He *peeled* five potatoes.
She is *peeling* an orange for the kids.

gloss: To rub food against a rough surface so it breaks into small shreds.
examples: *Grate* some parmesan over the pasta.
She *grated* a whole block of cheese.
He is *grating* carrots for the salad.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *great*; the -e drops before -ing: *grating*.

gloss: To press something hard so that it breaks into small pieces.
examples: *Crush* the garlic with the flat of the knife.
He *crushed* ice for the drinks.
She is *crushing* crackers for the topping.
contrast: -sh takes -es: *crushes*.

gloss: To crush cooked food into a soft mass.
examples: *Mash* the potatoes with butter and milk.
He *mashed* a banana for the baby.
She is *mashing* avocado for the guacamole.
contrast: -sh takes -es: *mashes*.

gloss: To beat cream or eggs quickly until they are light and thick.
examples: *Whip* the cream until it holds peaks.
She *whipped* the egg whites by hand.
He is *whipping* butter and sugar together.
contrast: The p doubles: *whipped*, *whipping* — as in *whipped cream*.

gloss: To mix or beat ingredients rapidly with a wire tool or a fork.
examples: *Whisk* the eggs with a little milk.
He *whisked* the sauce until it was smooth.
She is *whisking* batter for pancakes.

gloss: To press and fold dough with your hands until it is smooth.
examples: *Knead* the dough for ten minutes.
She *kneaded* it until it was springy.
He is *kneading* bread on the counter.
contrast: The k is silent: *knead* sounds exactly like *need*.

transitivity: both — transitive (roll the dough), intransitive (the meatball rolled off)
gloss: To flatten dough with a rolling pin, or to wrap food into a tube shape.
examples: *Roll* the dough out thin.
She *rolled* it into a circle.
He is *rolling* sushi at the counter.
contrast: Sounds like *role*, a completely different word.

gloss: To break the shell of an egg or a nut open.
examples: *Crack* two eggs into the bowl.
He *cracked* the eggs one-handed.
She is *cracking* walnuts for the cake.

transitivity: both — transitive (crumble the cheese), intransitive (the cookie crumbled)
gloss: To break food into small crumbs, or to fall apart into them.
examples: *Crumble* the feta over the salad.
He *crumbled* bacon on top.
The cornbread was *crumbling* in my hands.

transitivity: both — transitive (stir the soup), intransitive (stir until smooth)
gloss: To move a liquid or mixture around with a spoon.
examples: *Stir* the soup so it doesn't stick.
She *stirred* sugar into her tea.
He is *stirring* the risotto constantly.
contrast: The r doubles: *stirred*, *stirring*.

transitivity: both — transitive (mix the batter), intransitive (oil and water don't mix)
gloss: To combine two or more ingredients into one.
examples: *Mix* the dry ingredients first.
She *mixed* the batter by hand.
He is *mixing* a drink for you.
contrast: -x takes -es in the third person: *mixes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (pour the milk), intransitive (pour from the jug)
gloss: To make a liquid flow from one container into another.
examples: *Pour* the milk slowly.
He *poured* everyone a glass of wine.
She is *pouring* coffee for the table.
contrast: Rhymes with *more*; the sound-alike *pore* is a tiny hole in the skin.

gloss: To lift food out with a spoon or a deep utensil.
examples: *Scoop* the ice cream into bowls.
He *scooped* the seeds out of the pumpkin.
She is *scooping* rice onto each plate.

gloss: To fill a glass or a container again.
examples: Waiters here *refill* your coffee for free.
She *refilled* my water twice.
He is *refilling* the pitcher.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (ree-FIL); the noun *a refill* on the first.

transitivity: both — transitive (brew coffee), intransitive (the tea is brewing)
gloss: To make tea, coffee, or beer by steeping or fermenting.
examples: I *brew* coffee every morning at six.
She *brewed* a pot of green tea.
That beer is *brewed* in Vermont.

transitivity: both — transitive (steep the tea), intransitive (let it steep)
gloss: To leave tea or herbs in hot water so that the flavor comes out.
examples: *Steep* the tea for three minutes.
He *steeped* the leaves too long and it turned bitter.
The tea has been *steeping* since you left.
contrast: Also a common adjective meaning 'sharply sloped': *a steep hill*.

gloss: To make a liquid weaker by adding water to it.
examples: *Dilute* the syrup with cold water.
He *diluted* the juice for the children.
The soup tasted *diluted* after all that broth.

transitivity: both — transitive (measure the flour), intransitive (the pan measures ten inches)
gloss: To find or take an exact amount of an ingredient.
examples: *Measure* the flour — don't guess.
She *measured* two cups of milk.
He is *measuring* the sugar now.
contrast: The s sounds like the s in *pleasure*: MEZH-ur.

transitivity: both — transitive (weigh the flour), intransitive (it weighs a pound)
gloss: To find how heavy something is, or to have a certain weight.
examples: *Weigh* the dough before you divide it.
He *weighed* the fish at the counter.
That turkey *weighs* fourteen pounds.
contrast: Spelled -eigh but pronounced WAY; the forms are *weighs*, *weighed*, *weighing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (soak the beans), intransitive (the rice soaks for an hour)
gloss: To leave food or dishes in liquid for a long time.
examples: *Soak* the beans overnight.
She *soaked* the rice for twenty minutes.
The pans are *soaking* in the sink.

transitivity: both — transitive (drain the pasta), intransitive (let the spinach drain)
gloss: To let liquid run off food or out of a container.
examples: *Drain* the pasta, but save a cup of the water.
He *drained* the can of beans.
The spinach is *draining* in the colander.

gloss: To pour a liquid through a sieve to take out the solid pieces.
examples: *Strain* the broth into a clean pot.
She *strained* the tea leaves out.
He is *straining* the stock through cheesecloth.

gloss: To wash something quickly with clean water.
examples: *Rinse* the rice until the water runs clear.
He *rinsed* the lettuce twice.
She is *rinsing* the plates before loading them.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *rinsing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (wash the dishes), intransitive (wash before dinner)
gloss: To clean something with water, usually with soap.
examples: *Wash* your hands before you cook.
He *washed* the dishes after dinner.
She is *washing* grapes at the sink.
contrast: -sh takes -es: *washes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (clear the table), intransitive (we cleared up after dinner)
gloss: To take dishes and food off a table.
examples: Let's *clear* the table before dessert.
She *cleared* the plates while we talked.
He is *clearing* the last of the glasses.

transitivity: both — transitive (clean the grill), intransitive (she cleans on Saturdays)
gloss: To remove dirt or food from something.
examples: *Clean* the grill while it's still warm.
He *cleaned* the kitchen after the party.
She is *cleaning* the counters.

gloss: To rub a surface with a cloth to clean or dry it.
examples: *Wipe* the table, please.
He *wiped* his mouth with a napkin.
She is *wiping* down the counter.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *wiping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (scrub the pan), intransitive (scrub harder)
gloss: To rub something hard with a brush or cloth to clean it.
examples: *Scrub* the potatoes under cold water.
He *scrubbed* the burnt pan for ten minutes.
She is *scrubbing* the cutting board.
contrast: The b doubles: *scrubbed*, *scrubbing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (dry the glasses), intransitive (the herbs dried in a week)
gloss: To remove the water from something.
examples: *Dry* the lettuce before you dress it.
He washed and *dried* every glass.
The herbs are *drying* by the window.
contrast: The -y becomes -ie- in *dries* and *dried*, but stays in *drying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (fill the pot), intransitive (the restaurant fills up by seven)
gloss: To put enough of something into a container to make it full.
examples: *Fill* the pot with cold water.
She *filled* our glasses to the top.
He is *filling* the kettle.
contrast: Takes **with** for the contents: *fill the glass with* water.

gloss: To treat food so that it can be kept for a long time.
examples: Salt and smoke *preserve* meat.
Her grandmother *preserved* peaches every August.
These lemons are *preserved* in salt.

gloss: To keep vegetables in vinegar or salty water so that they last and taste sour.
examples: You can *pickle* almost any vegetable.
He *pickled* a jar of cucumbers.
She is *pickling* red onions for the tacos.
contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: *pickling*.

gloss: To reach the end of the period when food is safe to eat or a coupon can be used.
examples: Milk *expires* fast in the summer.
The yogurt *expired* last week.
This coupon is *expiring* tomorrow.
contrast: The date on the carton is the *expiration* date — Americans rarely say 'expiry'.

transitivity: both — transitive (treat your friends), intransitive (put that away, I'll treat)
gloss: To pay for someone else's meal or drink.
examples: Put your wallet away — I'll *treat*.
He *treated* us to dinner after the game.
She is *treating* everyone to ice cream.
contrast: The thing follows **to**: *treat someone to* dinner.

transitivity: both — transitive (suck the juice out), intransitive (suck on a candy)
gloss: To draw liquid or a piece of food into your mouth with your lips.
examples: Don't *suck* the juice straight out of the box.
She *sucked* her soda through a straw.
He was *sucking* on a cough drop.
contrast: With candy or a straw it takes **on**: *suck on* a lozenge.

transitivity: both — transitive (flip the pancakes), intransitive (the burger flipped onto the coals)
gloss: To turn food over quickly so that the other side cooks.
examples: *Flip* the pancakes when they bubble.
He *flipped* the burgers one by one.
She is *flipping* an omelet in the pan.
contrast: The p doubles: *flipped*, *flipping*.

gloss: To heat an oven to the right temperature before the food goes in.
examples: *Preheat* the oven to three hundred fifty degrees.
I *preheated* the oven while I mixed the batter.
The oven is still *preheating*.

transitivity: both — transitive (broil the fish), intransitive (the chicken is broiling)
gloss: To cook food with strong heat coming from above, as in an American oven.
examples: *Broil* the fish for four minutes.
She *broiled* the cheese until it bubbled.
The chicken is *broiling* now.
contrast: American *broil* (heat from above) is what the British call *grill*.

transitivity: both — transitive (cool the syrup), intransitive (let the pie cool)
gloss: To become less hot, or to make something less hot.
examples: Let the pie *cool* before you cut it.
The soup *cooled* while we talked.
The cookies are *cooling* on a rack.

gloss: To give a particular taste to food or drink.
examples: A little vanilla *flavors* the whole batch.
She *flavored* the water with cucumber and mint.
This oil is *flavored* with chili.
contrast: American *flavor*, *flavored*; the British spelling is *flavour*.

gloss: To put food into a bag or box to take with you.
examples: I *pack* a lunch most days.
She *packed* sandwiches for the trip.
He is *packing* leftovers for tomorrow.

gloss: To add salt to food.
examples: *Salt* the water before the pasta goes in.
He *salted* the fries twice.
She is *salting* the meat before it goes on the grill.
contrast: The l is pronounced: SAWLT, not 'sawt'.

gloss: To make food or drink taste sweeter.
examples: *Sweeten* the tea with honey instead of sugar.
She *sweetened* the sauce with a little maple syrup.
This yogurt is *sweetened* with fruit.

gloss: To cook food for too long, so that it turns dry or mushy.
examples: Don't *overcook* the shrimp.
He *overcooked* the pasta again.
The steak was badly *overcooked*.

transitivity: both — transitive (sniff the milk), intransitive (the dog sniffed around the table)
gloss: To draw air in through your nose in order to smell something.
examples: *Sniff* the milk before you pour it.
She *sniffed* the carton and made a face.
He is *sniffing* the wine in his glass.
